planting.note: Divide stoloniferous offsets in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil under deciduous canopy, matching its native cove-forest and rock-outcrop habitat.

directions: Carved out of the old Tiarella cordifolia complex in a 2021 taxonomic split, this stoloniferous foamflower is adapted to the warmer summers of the southern Blue Ridge escarpment and Cumberland Plateau, giving Southeastern gardeners a correctly-named regional-provenance groundcover instead of a generic northern selection. It spreads steadily by stolons to knit a weed-suppressing mat under hardwood canopy, so give it room to run or edge the bed to contain it. Because the species was only recently distinguished, source plants from a native-plant specialist carrying verified Southern Appalachian material.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide congested colonies in early spring into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil at pH 5.5-6.5 in part to full shade.

directions: The widest-ranging of the five species split from Tiarella cordifolia in 2021, running from Nova Scotia to Ontario and south into the Appalachians, this is very likely the taxon already dominating the commercial 'foamflower' nursery trade under the older, broader name. Its running stolons make it the most reliable large-area woodland groundcover in the genus, useful for naturalizing under mature trees where slower cultivars would take years to fill in. Divide crowded colonies in early spring to rejuvenate the planting and start new drifts elsewhere.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Transplant young divisions while small, since the species resents root disturbance once established, into moist, humus-rich clay or loam in dappled shade along a woodland edge or streambank.

directions: A clump-forming woodland wildflower of East Texas bottomland hardwood and riparian forest plus Hill Country limestone woods, this species gives Texas and Gulf gardeners a straight species native to their own region as a companion to the more easterly Spigelia marilandica. Flowers are white, often suffused with pink and marked with faint lavender lines, smaller and less dramatically bicolor than its red-and-yellow eastern relative, but it fills the same woodland-floor niche further west. Site it where it won't be disturbed after the first year, since like its relatives it is slow to settle in and resents transplanting once mature.
